name: Felix Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers are confidential. What does a usual shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the road grader at Iron Vale mine and lead the small crew that keeps haul roads passable. My two-year technical diploma helped, but twenty years feeling the blade taught me more. My partner and I have grown children and about three months of expenses saved. I have never used an AI tool, and I do not care to learn one for a job the grader already does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that if AI just tidies office forms, we should keep the roads smooth and get on with it. I would still inspect the blade and the drainage after rain. A shortcut on the road can cost a truck its tyres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my grader shifts and typical pay to continue. Three months of savings and a couple of other mines nearby give us room if a machine is out. I would still check our pension figures because retirement is getting close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the same grading route and inspect the culverts each Monday. I would request an updated pension statement this year and read it with my partner. I would leave office software to the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The road and household bills look manageable in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does a culvert problem first show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Water sits at the south turn before the surface breaks. I would clear that drain and mark the soft edge for truck drivers. A smooth-looking road can hide a wet hole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask for the pension statement now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am fifty-eight and would like to choose a date with my partner. Three months of savings is useful, but it is not a pension. I want the monthly income figure before promising anything.

say: I would keep **haul roads** smooth while AI handles small office forms.
I would continue the **Monday culvert check** after rain.
think: My **grader shifts** and typical pay look steady, with three months saved.
I need a **pension figure** before choosing when to retire.
do: **Keep** grading Iron Vale haul roads and checking culverts.
**Request** a pension statement and review it with my partner this year.
S0.quote: A smooth-looking road can hide a wet hole.
fieldNote: His **skill** is reading road surface and blade feel, with no AI use.
Typical pay, **three months saved** and some nearby mines make the mild picture secure.
He seeks a **pension statement** because of age, not a new technology scare.

steps.text: Keep grading Iron Vale haul roads and checking culverts
Request pension statement before choosing retirement date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say buying and planning software can help the office, but the grader crew still has to see the road. I would ask the foreman to keep our inspection time on the roster. An apprentice needs time beside the machine, not a faster worksheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own shifts look safe while robots spread slowly. The danger is a planner setting a route on a dry-day map and forgetting the wet south turn. I would be uneasy if the office trimmed a junior place, but I do not expect my wage to fall soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my road checks and ask for the new route plan on paper. I would mark wet patches and compare the schedule with actual trip times for a month. If the apprentice shift vanished, I would raise it with the foreman before accepting more road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can work with a new route, but I do not want the map to teach the apprentice what a puddle feels like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you mark on the paper plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The soft south turn and the culvert that fills after heavy rain. I would walk the apprentice there. A dry map cannot tell a new driver where the road gives way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the software yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would ask for a printout and check it on the road. If the mine required a screen, I would need somebody to show me slowly. I would not volunteer to test it.

say: I would keep **inspection time** on the road roster when office planning changes.
I would teach the **apprentice** at the wet south turn.
think: My **own wage** looks safe while hands-on robots spread slowly.
A dry-day **route plan** could miss hazards and erase junior learning time.
do: **Mark** wet patches on the printed route plan for one month.
**Ask** the foreman to restore the apprentice shift if a new roster removes it.
feel: **Uneasy** about road safety and apprentice time.
S1.quote: A dry map cannot tell a new driver where the road gives way.
fieldNote: He sees **office planning** changing before grader operation.
He does not claim to learn AI; he asks for a **printout** and checks it physically.
His worry is **safety and apprenticeship**, while his own income still appears secure.

steps.text: Keep checking Iron Vale roads against printed route plans
Review new roster before deciding whether to challenge apprentice cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that full thinking AI by 2028 changes planning first, while capable robot graders come around 2031. Iron Vale might buy them, and then an experienced driver could lose a seat. I would ask for the equipment schedule in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty when the planning changes and sixty-three when robot graders become capable. I might not be ready to retire at sixty-three, even with three months saved. If the mine cut my wage, a nearby mine might offer work, but I would check before counting on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would delay replacing our car and request a pension estimate this month. I would keep grading after 2028 while human drivers are still needed. I would ask the foreman about paid grader-repair training, and enrol only if a real maintenance post was listed and my wages continued.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I could make a plan, but a possible lost wage at sixty-three would be hard to ignore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask a nearby mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether they planned to buy robot graders and whether they had a paid road job. I would not move for a vacancy that lasted one season. My partner and I would compare the pay and travel time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children help with retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They would help in an emergency, but they have their own households. I would rather work a few more years than make my grown children our regular bill payers. We can talk honestly without handing them the problem.

say: I would distinguish **2028 planning AI** from capable robot graders around 2031.
I would request a **written equipment schedule** before changing retirement plans.
think: At **sixty-three**, losing grader wages could come before affordable retirement.
Three months saved gives some room, but a **nearby vacancy** may not last.
do: **Delay** replacing the car and request a pension estimate this month.
**Keep** grading after 2028 while human drivers remain.
**Enrol** in paid grader-repair training only if a maintenance post is listed and wages continue.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible wage loss at sixty-three.
S2.quote: I would rather work a few more years than make my grown children our regular bill payers.
fieldNote: He separates **2028 planning** from capable robot graders around 2031.
His **three-month cushion** permits planning but may not cover early retirement.
Repair training requires a **listed post**, paid instruction and continued wages.

steps.text: Delay replacing the household car this year
Keep grading Iron Vale roads after 2028 while drivers remain
Enrol in paid grader repair training if post listed and wages continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years to thinking AI and roughly eight to capable robot graders gives us time to teach younger drivers well. The mine should publish trial dates. I would ask the foreman to keep the road apprentice on a proper wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-three when planning AI arrives in 2031 and about sixty-six when robot graders become capable in 2034. We might be able to retire by then if the pension is sound. I would still worry if my shifts ended before the numbers worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request pension projections for ages sixty-five and sixty-seven and compare them with our monthly bills. I would keep training the apprentice on wet roads. If the mine posted paid road-inspection work and funded instruction, I would take that training while keeping my grader wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I have more years to decide, but the pension figures still have to be checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would road inspection add to your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already spot bad drainage; the formal role would need written reports and sign-off rules. I could learn those with a paid teacher. I would not buy a certificate just to sit in a classroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension is short at sixty-six?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would work the grader longer if Iron Vale still needed me. A road-inspection post could help if the grader shifts shrank. I would not retire from grading at Iron Vale mine on a guess.

say: I would ask for **trial dates** and a paid road apprentice before capable robots around 2034.
I would keep **wet-road teaching** on the crew schedule.
think: At about **sixty-six**, retirement could work if monthly pension income covers bills.
Early loss of **grader shifts** would still be a risk.
do: **Compare** pension projections for sixty-five and sixty-seven with monthly bills.
**Take** funded road-inspection instruction if a paid post opens and grader wages continue.
feel: **Uneasy**, pending pension figures and posted work.
S3.quote: I would not retire from grading at Iron Vale mine on a guess.
fieldNote: He would be **sixty-three** at thinking AI and about sixty-six when robots become capable.
His **road-inspection training** requires funding, a paid post and continued grader wages.
He wants to keep teaching even if **retirement** may arrive before the robot date.

steps.text: Compare pension projections at sixty-five and sixty-seven with bills
Keep teaching apprentice wet-road checks on current shifts
Take funded road-inspection instruction if paid post opens with wages continuing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade to thinking AI and about thirteen years to capable robot graders is enough time for a sensible equipment plan. I would ask Iron Vale to publish one. Young drivers should learn the road properly while people still run the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-eight in 2036 and about seventy-one when robot graders become capable in 2039. I expect to be retired by then if our pension pays what the statement suggests. Three months of savings help, but I would check the figures every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep grading and teaching the apprentice now. I would request an annual pension statement and review it with my partner. I would also show the younger drivers the south turn after rain before they take it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our own income path, provided the pension stays on track. I would be more concerned for drivers who have decades of work ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire early when the mine begins a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would base the date on the pension and my partner’s plans. A robot grader trial announcement by itself does not pay bills. I might work to the date we already chose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a young driver?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep your eyes on the road, learn the machine, and save some wages. A printed plan is useful, but the wet south turn still needs a careful hand. I would show the turn before giving advice.

say: I would ask Iron Vale for a **published equipment plan** during the long warning.
I would keep **young drivers** learning the wet road while people still operate graders.
think: At about **seventy-one**, I expect retirement before capable robots if pension income holds.
Our **three-month cushion** helps, though I would still check figures yearly.
do: **Keep** grading and teaching the road apprentice.
**Request** an annual pension statement and review it with my partner.
feel: **Calm** about household income if the pension path holds.
S4.quote: A robot grader trial announcement by itself does not pay bills.
fieldNote: The **2039 robot date** falls near age seventy-one, when planned retirement appears feasible.
He remains **resistant to AI tools** while using printed plans and physical road lessons.
His advice to young drivers reflects **work and saving**, not a policy campaign.

steps.text: Keep grading Iron Vale roads and teaching apprentice
Request annual pension statement before confirming retirement date

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robot graders could appear around 2031, before I have settled a retirement date. A written equipment schedule and funded repair instruction tied to real posts would help. I would also want a clear pension estimate.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who teaches the road after the first robot trial. I know where rain pools on the south turn, but that knowledge is not stored in a printer. Young drivers need a paid teacher before robot graders take over the haul roads.

headlineQuote: Young drivers need a paid teacher before robot graders take over the haul roads.
portrait: Felix Okafor is a **58-year-old** road-grader lead at Iron Vale mine, with a technical diploma, grown children and three months saved.
He has **typical pay** and some nearby mine options, but needs pension figures before choosing a retirement date.
He avoids **AI tools**, checks printed routes against wet roads and insists younger drivers receive paid, physical instruction.
Fast capable robots make him **anxious** about wages; a longer warning makes retirement more plausible if pension income holds.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because capable robot graders could arrive around 2031 before retirement is settled.
whatWouldHelp: A **written schedule**, funded repair instruction tied to real posts and a clear pension estimate would help.
